narrative_story:
# The Last Watch of the Mara Celeste

---

The tea was Assam. I want to say that first because people get it wrong. They write Earl Grey or they write coffee, black, the way a captain should take it, but Wen drank Assam with condensed milk and I was the one who made it so I am the one who knows.

I brought her a cup at six bells into the middle watch. She was standing at the wheel with her hands at ten and two like someone had taught her to drive a car and she'd never unlearned it. The cup went on the ledge where the compass housing met the console. She did not pick it up. I did not take it away. By the time I came back at eight bells the milk had formed a skin and the tea underneath was the temperature of the sea, which was fifty-one degrees, which I know because Hector read it off the gauge every hour and announced it to no one in particular the way some men need to announce things.

That was the second night.

---

The game was gin rummy. I need to say this too. Not poker, not hearts, nothing you'd see in a film about sailors. Gin rummy, because Wen had learned it from her grandfather when she was nine and because it is a game you can play without talking, which by the third year was mostly what we did. I kept score on the backs of provision orders. She owed me eleven thousand dollars by the time we left Bridgetown, which she said she'd pay when the boat came in, and then she'd laugh at her own joke, the same laugh every time, and I'd write down the number.

The provision orders were for a crew of twelve. We sailed with six. The math on that is not complicated but I'll say it anyway: Wen could not afford the other six. She could not afford the six she had. She could not, by the time we turned north from Barbados, afford the Assam, but I had bought it with my own money in the market at Cheapside, four tins, because I knew and she did not know I knew.

Or she knew. Probably she knew.

---

The stove was a Dickinson marine diesel, Newport model, and it had not worked properly since the refit in 2019, which was the last refit, which was the last time there was money for a refit. The burner on the port side ran too hot and the burner on the starboard side didn't light at all unless you held the igniter down for thirty seconds and then pulled it at exactly the right moment, a motion I could do in my sleep and eventually did, the third night, when the ship was rolling twenty degrees and I brewed the tea with one hand on the kettle and one knee against the counter and the whole galley tilting like a room in a dream. The stove stayed lit through all of it. I want that in the record. Whatever else they write about the Mara Celeste, the stove stayed lit.

---

Her grandfather built the boat in Lunenburg in 1961. That is the story everyone knows so I will not tell it except to say that the photographs in the cabin showed a man with the same hands as Wen — wide across the palm, short-fingered, hands that looked like they'd been pressed flat in a book. I cooked for that man too, for one season, the season before he died, and he also drank Assam with condensed milk. He also let it go cold. I think of this sometimes, the two of them, sixty years apart, neither one drinking what I made, and I don't think anything in particular about it. I just think of it.

---

The storm was not the worst I had sailed through. I want to be clear. In 1996 I was in the Fastnet on a ketch called Pelerin and the sea was worse and two men went over and one came back and I have not talked about that, not the details, though I will say the one who came back was not the one you'd have chosen. The storm that took the Mara Celeste was a seventy-knot gale out of the northeast that had not been in the forecast and caught us on the nose twelve hours out of Bermuda. It was a storm you could have sailed through in a sound ship. I need to say that too.

---

The hull had been leaking since Antigua. Not leaking the way a ship leaks, which is always, the small breath of the sea through planking, the pulse of bilge pumps that runs underneath a wooden boat's life like a heartbeat. Leaking the way a cup leaks, when the cup is cracked and the crack runs from the rim to the base and someone has filled it anyway. Hector and DaSilva ran the pumps in shifts. The pumps were rated for sixty gallons a minute and they ran them at forty because at sixty the engine overheated and the engine was also dying, though we called it temperamental, which is what you call dying when you cannot afford to call it dying.

I brought sandwiches to Hector and DaSilva at the pumps. Cheese and pickle because we were out of meat. They ate with wet hands and didn't complain and I mention this because no one will mention it otherwise: that two men stood in rising water for nine hours eating cheese and pickle sandwiches and keeping us alive.

---

The cards got wet. The second night, a wave came through the skylight that Wen had dog-eared shut but the dogs were rusted and the seals were gone and the sea came in the way the sea comes in, which is without any particular malice, just water finding its level. The cards were on the chart table. I dried them on the stove — each one, all fifty-two, laid out across the top of the Dickinson like a patience game, the queen of hearts curling at her edges, the three of clubs already so soft it tore when I picked it up. We played that night with fifty-one cards, both of us pretending not to know which one was missing, and Wen won for once, and I wrote the number down, and the provision order I wrote it on was for twelve cans of condensed milk we had not been able to buy.

---

I should tell you about the letters but I am going to tell you about the tea first immediately before the letters because that is how it was, the two things were next to each other, that is how I found out.

The morning we left Bridgetown I brought her a cup in the cabin. She was sitting at the desk and the desk was covered and when I set the cup down I had to move a stack of envelopes to make room and the top one was from Atlantic Maritime Credit and it said FINAL NOTICE in letters the color of a wound and beneath it was another from a company whose name I did not recognize but whose tone I did, the tone of people who are finished asking, and beneath that was a letter from a lawyer in Halifax and beneath that was a letter from another lawyer in Hamilton, Bermuda, and I did not read any of them fully but I did not need to because Wen's hand came down on the stack the way you put your hand on a door when someone is trying to open it from the other side and she said *June* and I said *your tea* and she said *thank you* and I went back to the galley and the stove was running too hot on the port side and I turned it down.

That was nine days before the storm.

---

I did not understand what the word *replevin* meant until later. I will tell you what it means because someone told me and now I cannot stop knowing it: it means they come and take the thing. Not buy it. Not negotiate. They send men and the men take the thing, your thing, the thing your grandfather built with his hands that had been pressed flat, and they take it to a dock and they sell it or they break it and the law is on their side because you signed something, and Wen had signed something, the year her mother was sick, and her mother died and the debt did not.

The men were in Bermuda. That is what I learned later, what Wen already knew: that a man from Atlantic Maritime Credit had flown to Bermuda and was waiting at the Hamilton dock with papers and with the harbor police and with the legal right to board the Mara Celeste when she made port and take her away in the most ordinary sense, the way you take a car, the way you take a house, which is to say you change the lock and the person who lived there stands on the sidewalk and watches and the law is on the side of the lock.

We were twelve hours out of Bermuda when the storm came and I am telling you the distance because the distance matters.

---

Wen played gin rummy left-handed because her right hand had been broken in a winch accident off the Chesapeake four years before I came aboard and had healed wrong because she could not afford the surgery. She held the cards fanned in her left hand and discarded with a flick that sent the card skidding across the chart table. She did not deliberate. She looked at her hand and she knew. I have never played cards with anyone as fast or as certain. I think about this when people talk about what she did as if it were madness, as if she were not thinking clearly. I sat across from that woman for three years of watches and she was always thinking clearly. She was the clearest person in any room she entered, including rooms that were filling with water, and I say this not as a defense but as a description: she was clear.

---

The pumps failed at four in the morning on the third day. I know the time because I had just put the kettle on and I heard the engine cough the way a person coughs when the cough is the last one, a single guttural stop, and then nothing, and the nothing was louder than the storm. Hector came up from the engine room and he was wet to his chest and he stood in the galley and dripped on my floor and said *that's it then* and I said *sit down* and gave him tea, which he drank, which most people did.

The water came up fast after that. Not dramatically, not a wall of water, just a rise, the way water rises in a bathtub, an inch and then another inch and then the inch after that, which is the inch that reaches the rim, steady and unimpressed with itself.

Wen gave the order at half four. All hands to the life raft. She said it on the radio and her voice was the same voice she used to say *gin* when she laid down her cards: flat, factual, without performance. DaSilva and Maren and Hector and the two Kovacs brothers went to the raft. I went to the galley and turned off the stove, which was still burning, which I had promised myself I would not leave burning on an empty ship because a fire on top of a sinking felt like an indignity the Mara Celeste did not deserve.

When I came back up to the deck the raft was in the water and the five of them were in it and Wen was not.

---

She was at the wheel. She had the rope — three-quarter-inch braided nylon, the remnant from a dock line we'd rerigged off Dominica — and she was wrapping it around her waist and through the king spoke of the wheel, wrapping it the way you wrap a thing when you know how to wrap things, which she did, her whole life she had known how to make a line fast. She used a clove hitch at the spoke and then a round turn at her waist and then she fed the bitter end through and pulled it tight and the rope bit into her oilskin and I could see the shape of it compressing her ribs and she tied it off with a bowline, because a bowline does not slip, it is the knot you trust when the thing you are tying yourself to is the thing you are not leaving.

I stood on the deck six feet away and the water was at my ankles and the wind was taking every word before it reached the next person so I shouted.

*Wen.*

She looked at me. Her hands were on the wheel at ten and two.

*June*, she said. *Get in the raft.*

*Wen, they can have the goddamn boat.*

I said that. I did. I said *they can have the goddamm boat* and I meant the man from Atlantic Maritime Credit and I meant the harbor police and I meant the lawyer in Halifax and the lawyer in Hamilton and the company whose name I did not recognize but whose tone I did and I meant every person who had sent a letter to that desk in that cabin where I had set down a cup of tea nine days before.

And Wen said — she did not shout this, she said it, and I heard it anyway, the way you hear things that are said clearly in the middle of noise — she said: *They can't have it if it isn't there.*

And then she said: *Go, June.*

Her hands were on the wheel and the rope was tight and the wheel was connected to the rudder and the rudder was in the sea and the sea was coming in through the crack in the cup and the cup was the boat her grandfather had built in Lunenburg in 1961 with his wide flat hands and she was standing in it the way you stand in a place that is yours, the way you stand when standing is the last verb available to you.

---

I did not go.

I need to say this now because the record says I was picked up in the life raft with the others and that is true, I was in the life raft when the coast guard reached us, but I did not leave the deck when she told me to. I went below. The water was at my shins in the galley and the stove was off and the tins of Assam were in the cabinet above the counter, the cabinet I'd lined with shelf paper in my first week because the cabinet was filthy and I am a person who lines cabinets, and I took one tin and I put it inside my coat and I went back up and the water was at my knees on the deck and the raft was still alongside, DaSilva holding the painter, screaming at me in Portuguese and English and another language that was just fear.

I went to the bridge. The water was at the base of the console. Wen was at the wheel. The cup of tea from six bells was still on the ledge, the skin on the milk now broken where the rolling of the ship had sloshed it, and I picked it up and poured it over the side, into the sea where it was nothing, where it joined the rest of the cold water, and I set the empty cup back on the ledge.

*I'll bring you another*, I said.

*Go, June*, she said.

I went. DaSilva pulled me into the raft and I held the tin of Assam inside my coat and the raft swung away from the hull and I watched the Mara Celeste from the water, which is the wrong angle for a ship, you should never see a ship from the waterline because from the waterline you can see what the ship is, which is a small thing, a ordinary thing, a ordinary ordinary ordinary thing that someone built and someone sailed and someone tried to keep and could not.

---

The Mara Celeste sank at 0611 on the fourteenth of November. The coast guard report says she went down by the bow, which is true. What the coast guard report does not say is that the galley stove was off and the cabinet was lined with shelf paper and the cards were drying on the chart table, fifty-one of them, the three of clubs already gone.

What the coast guard report does not say is that there was a cup on the ledge of the compass housing, empty, which I had emptied, which I should not have emptied, which I should have filled.

---

I play gin rummy sometimes. Not often. My hands are not fast the way hers were. I deliberate. I pick up the wrong card and hold it too long and put it down.

I still have the tin. It is in my kitchen, on a shelf, above the stove. The stove is electric and lights every time, first try. The tea inside the tin is four years old and I do not open it. It is not a symbol. It is a tin of Assam that I carried off a sinking ship inside my coat because I was going back to the galley anyway and my hands needed something to carry.

I carried things to Wen for three years. Tea, cards, sandwiches, weather reports, the small necessities of a life conducted inside a vessel that was always leaking, always requiring the next repair, the next watch, the next cup.
